figures.caption: Figure 1: Attack success rate (ASR) leaderboard across backends, with a skill-domain zoom-in revealing opposite failure modes among the most robust models.

Table 1: Cross-backend attack-conditioned results (ASR %, lower is safer). ∆OSS is the attack-attributable output shift OSSattack−OSSbaseline, reported separately for failed (ASR=0) and successful (ASR=1) cases (negative values indicate a more conservative response than the clean baseline); SS is the blind-auditor stealth score over the same two sub-populations. Higher-ASR cells use gray fill with progressively stronger typography (bold; bold+underline). Dashes mark no successful cases. Backends sorted by overall ASR. Vendor references are in Appendix A.2.

Figure 2: Overview of SEARCHGEO. (a) Benign queries from four high-stakes domains. (b) A three-layer attack taxonomy (machine-layer 1A/1B, trust-signal 2A/2B, compound 3); the example shows Mode 2B replacing the top three returned results. (c) The search agent issues queries to a hybrid search proxy that returns either injected or clean results, with live fallback for off-cluster queries. The answer is scored on ASR, OSS, SS, and optionally FRR.

Figure 3: Attack success rate by the number of injected sources N on Gemini-3-Flash. Repeating the same source in Mode 2A remains approximately flat, whereas adding distinct corroborating sources in Modes 2B and 3 sharply increases endorsement corruption.
Table 8: Backend display names, API routes, and exact model identifiers used for the main cross-backend experiments. The same identifiers are used for the auxiliary probes unless otherwise stated.

Table 13: Silent-shift incidence by backend, using attack-attributable drift. n is the number of attack cases (excluding the clean baseline); ASR=0 is the number of non-endorsement cases; Silent counts ASR= 0 cases where ∆OSS≥0.3 (attack moved the answer by more than one OSS-rubric tier on top of the clean-baseline answer for the same backend and task); Rate = Silent/n. Backends are ordered as in Table 1.

Table 15: Attack-only ASR by backend and domain. Values are percentages; clean-baseline cases are excluded. Backends are ordered as in Table 1. Legal and Consumer IT are the most attacked domains on average, but the most-exposed domain varies by model (e.g., Gemini-3-Flash peaks on Legal at 43.9%, while Qwen3.6-Plus peaks on Consumer IT at 31.8%).

Table 14: Attack-attributable shift ∆OSS = OSSattack − OSSbaseline conditional on ASR=0, per backend and domain. n is the number of ASR=0 attack cases per cell; mean and max are over ∆OSS values within the cell; ≥ .3 counts cases where the attack added at least one OSS-rubric tier of drift on top of the clean baseline. Negative mean values indicate that, on average, attack content triggered a more conservative response than the clean baseline. Backends are ordered as in Table 1.

Table 9: Backend-level search behavior in the main experiment, including the 44 clean-baseline cases and 264 attack-conditioned cases per backend. Search-call counts are exact counts from raw traces. Live follow-up counts estimate searches that escaped the cached SEO coverage and were routed to clean SerpAPI fallback.

Table 12: Within-family failure-set overlap on the 264 attack cases. A case is keyed by attack mode, domain, and query ID. A is the lower-ASR member in each pair as ordered in Table 11; |A \B| = 0 indicates that the lower-ASR model’s failures are fully contained in the higher-ASR model’s failures.

Table 18: ∆ from condition A (percentage points). Positive values mean more ASR than the no-defense baseline. The two boldface cells highlight where condition C amplifies attacks on Gemini while reducing them on the other two backends.

Table 17: Per-mode ASR (%) by backend and condition. A = no defense, B = OWASP-derived unified-defense prompt, C = OpenClaw stock workspace with minimum-required modifications (per-call session, anti-NO_REPLY clarifier, search mandate). The final row is the average over attack modes only and excludes the clean baseline. Bold cells mark where condition C increases ASR by >5pp relative to condition A on that mode.
